author: TEDx Talks
description:
Do you think you are at risk of adopting an extremist ideology? Most of us would say, of course not! Yet in this illuminating talk, political neuroscientist Leor Zmigrod reveals that some people's brains have hidden characteristics that make them especially vulnerable to rigid, authoritarian beliefs. She shares strategies to make our brains more resilient and flexible, helping us resist extremism and live with greater adaptability, sensitivity, and authenticity.

[9:35] For more on the relationship between inequality justification and empathy, see here: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-14193-z

Leor is an award-winning cognitive scientist whose research on ideological extremism bridges the fields of psychology, neuroscience, and political science. A Gates Scholar at the University of Cambridge, she has held fellowships at Harvard, Stanford, and leading European institutes. Honored by Forbes 30 Under 30 and the American Political Science Association, she is a recognized voice
title: Are you susceptible to extremism? Take this cognitive test. | Leor Zmigrod | TEDxNewEngland

author: TEDx Talks
description:
Kweku introduces the science of Causal Inference — the discipline of moving beyond what happens together to understand why one thing produces another. Correlation tells us that two things move in step; causation tells us which lever actually pulls the world. That distinction, he argues, is the real seat of intelligence — in both human minds and the machines we're building. It's what separates pattern-matching from genuine understanding.

But his deeper claim is this: true intelligence lies in mapping the path from cause to consequence — in seeing how a single, intentional shift can ripple outward into a cascade of global impact. When we understand causes, we stop reacting to the world and start reshaping it. We learn where to push, and how one small, deliberate act can set the whole system in motion. From a corridor in Perth to Vienna in the 18th century, from Istanbul at dawn to a CNN documentary about the last Nazi hunter - music has always been humanity's most powerful vehicle for emotional travel. In this talk, Michael Pignéguy makes the case that this power isn't something that happens to you. It's something you can learn to use - and it starts with a single question: what is this music doing to me right now? The gap between feeling music and using it is where your personal soundtrack actually lives. Michael Pignéguy is a composer, performer and educator on a mission to explore how music shapes the way we experience the world. Over thirty years working across jazz, orchestral and world music - and across four continents - he has seen what music does to people. Including himself.

Why do donuts, social media and video games feel so rewarding? Dr Anastasia Hronis explores the hidden cost of dopamine-driven activities and the powers of oxytocin. Learn practical strategies to reclaim your brain and reconnect with what truly matters. Anastasia is a clinical psychologist, working across both clinical practice and academia. This talk shares a powerful personal journey from a high-paced corporate life to a turning point marked by illness, which became an invitation to look inward. It explores the idea that true wellness is not something we can buy or achieve by only treating symptoms, but rather an inside-out process rooted in emotional, mental, and physical alignment.
